open_obligations: Check that Hase et al.'s SGR uses training on hard data as the ceiling, so that exceeding it would break the metric
Check how often easy-only training actually exceeds full training in Sun et al.'s tables

Sun et al. compare easy-only training, particularly with RL, against training across all difficulty levels, not against Hase et al.'s finetuning on hard data, so their observation does not directly show easy-only training exceeding SGR's Hard term
out.other_title: Supervision Gap Recovered (SGR) metric for easy-to-hard generalization
out.rationale: The authors choose not to establish an SGR-style metric because models trained only on simpler tasks, particularly with RL training, can outperform those trained across the entire spectrum of problem difficulties, which shows a limit of the metric's applicability in their setting without a direct conflict with Hase et al.'s findings, so CHALLENGES. Hase et al.'s SGR compares finetuning on easy data, hard data, or no data (zero-shot).
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether a supervision-gap-recovered metric anchored on hard-data training is meaningful; holds where easy-only training can outperform training across the entire spectrum of problem difficulties

text: The authors choose not to use an analogue of the easy-to-hard supervision gap recovered (SGR) metric of Hase et al. They say models trained only on easier tasks, particularly with RL, can outperform those trained on all difficulty levels, so they focus on absolute and relative performance on MATH500.
title: Sun et al. decline Hase et al.'s SGR metric because easy-only training can beat full training
